look: Low wooden houses and shops with tiled roofs, and rows of white fireproof storehouses along the canals. The shogun's castle stood at the centre.
Everyone wore kimono. Samurai carried two swords; townspeople wore cotton kimono with straw sandals or wooden clogs, and straw hats against sun and rain.
On foot over hundreds of bridges, by boat along the canals, or carried in a small palanquin. Wheeled carriages for people were almost unknown.
Paper lanterns at doors and shops, and a hand lantern for anyone walking after dark.
About a million people lived in Edo, one of the largest cities in the world. Japan was closed to almost all foreigners.

stops.name: Nihonbashi, the heart of the city
stops.title: Nihonbashi in Edo, from Thirty-six Views of Mount Fuji
stops.note: A colour woodblock print by Hokusai, the artist of The Great Wave.

spots.d: Edo Castle, home of the shogun, the military ruler of Japan.
spots.how: Its moats and walls still surround the Imperial Palace in Tokyo.

spots.d: Japan's sacred mountain, about 100 kilometres away, could be seen from the city on clear days.
spots.how: Hokusai put Fuji into every picture in this series.

spots.d: Merchants kept their goods in thick white plaster storehouses, because fires often swept through the wooden city.
spots.how: Edo had so many great fires that people called them the flowers of Edo.

spots.d: Rice, fish, wood and other goods came into the city by boat.
spots.how: Canals linked the bay to the markets.

stops.name: The Mitsui shop at Surugachō
stops.title: Mitsui shop at Surugachō in Edo

spots.d: Workmen repair the tiled roof of the shop.
spots.how: Hokusai loved to show people at work.

spots.d: Flying kites was a favourite pastime, especially around New Year.
spots.how: Kites appear in many Edo prints.

spots.d: This was Echigoya, the Mitsui family's cloth shop, where customers paid a fixed price in cash. It grew into the Mitsukoshi department store.
spots.how: Mitsukoshi still stands on the same spot in Tokyo.

spots.d: The street was laid out so Mount Fuji appeared at its end.
spots.how: Hokusai framed the mountain between the shop roofs.

stops.name: Morning at Nihonbashi bridge
stops.title: Nihonbashi: Morning View, from Fifty-three Stations of the Tōkaidō

spots.d: Every other year each lord had to travel to Edo with a long procession of servants. Here one sets out at dawn.
spots.how: This rule, called sankin-kōtai, lasted until 1862.

spots.d: The procession carries tall feathered standards to show whose lord is passing.
spots.how: Hiroshige drew the real gear of these processions.

spots.d: Nihonbashi had Edo's fish market. Sellers carried fish in tubs hanging from a pole on their shoulders.
spots.how: The fish market stayed at Nihonbashi until 1923.

spots.d: Wooden gates closed off each neighbourhood at night.
spots.how: Guards opened them only for people with a good reason.

spots.d: Straw raincoats, umbrellas of oiled paper and big straw hats kept people dry.
spots.how: Hiroshige was famous for his rain.

spots.d: Nihonbashi was a wooden arched bridge, rebuilt many times after fires.
spots.how: The stone bridge there today dates from 1911.

spots.d: Boats crowd the river near the market.
spots.how: Goods for the markets came in by water.
